strengths: The core methodological contribution is well-motivated and carefully executed: rather than constructing bespoke GP priors restricted to RKHSs (as in BayesIMP), the authors relax the RKHS constraint (linear-kernel GP on f) and use Mercer/spectral representations of the feature map to reduce the infinite-dimensional conditional mean embedding to scalar GPs on coordinates. This yields tractable, closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1) and a posterior mean that provably coincides with the state-of-the-art kernel estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Section A.5), which is a strong design principle for UQ around an established estimator.

The theoretical development is unusually careful for a GP-methods paper: L^2-convergence of the IMPspec representation (Proposition 3), exchange of expectation with an unbounded linear functional (Lemma 4), Fubini/trace-class justifications in the proof of Theorem 1, and a consistency result for the bootstrap-based calibration estimator (Theorem 6).

The analysis of prior work (BayesIMP) is itself a valuable contribution: Propositions 1–2 formally characterize the nonstationarity/collapse of nuclear-dominant kernels causing underfitting, and Section A.6.2 explains the variance collapse of finite-dimensional approximations out-of-distribution, both backed by diagnostics (Figs. 3, 4, 5).

A novel and useful byproduct is the closed-form weighted log-likelihood objective (Eq. 21) for hyperparameters of the spectral-coordinate GPs, enabled by the spectral decomposition, plus a practical calibration procedure for the spectral measure (Algorithm 2).

Experiments include relevant baselines (BayesIMP, sampling GP, continuous doubly-robust), multiple estimands (ATE, CATE, ATT), ablations (spectral calibration on/off, sample splitting, MC-approximated BayesIMP kernels), and honest reporting — e.g., disclosing that they fixed typos in the BayesIMP implementation and that sample splitting matters for calibration.

Reproducibility is supported: code availability is stated, and implementation details are extensive (appendix C), including data-generating processes, kernel choices, optimization settings, and an extension of the method to causal data fusion (Section A.4, Algorithm 3).
weaknesses: The object is called a 'process' but γ is not a Gaussian process; inference relies on a KL-optimal moment-matched Gaussian surrogate (Section 4.2). Credible intervals are Gaussian quantiles on a non-Gaussian process; coverage claims rest on the (heuristic, grid-search-based) spectral calibration, and the consistency result (Theorem 6) requires smoothness and sample-splitting conditions whose practical impact is only partially explored.

Positivity of the derived posterior variance (S1 + S2 + S3) is not established — S1 = β(z)^T K_V (I k_W(w,w) − A(w)K_V) β(z) need not be obviously nonnegative (A(w)K_V is not symmetric), and the paper does not discuss whether the moment expressions can yield invalid (negative) variances or how the surrogate behaves then.

Empirical scale and realism are limited: all experiments use n = 100 (or 500) on synthetic settings; the 'healthcare application' is in fact a simulator (with a linear PSA→VOL model fit to published statistics), not real patient data. Scalability claims (O(n^3), stochastic-gradient suggestions for n ≥ 10^4) are not validated empirically.

Baselines are narrow: the main comparison is against BayesIMP (which the paper shows to be defective) and one doubly-robust estimator; comparisons against other CATE/dose-response UQ methods (e.g., semiparametric CATE interval methods, heteroskedastic GP baselines) are absent, making 'state-of-the-art' claims hard to fully substantiate.

The spectral measure ν is a free modeling choice that controls posterior variance; the parametric family used (ν_β = N(V̄, β²I)) and grid search over β is somewhat ad hoc, and the calibration criterion (Eq. 22) targets average coverage over user-specified test grids, which may not transfer to other regions of the treatment space.

Minor presentation issues: several typos in the appendix (e.g., 'Vdar', mismatched brackets in trace expressions, the S3 definition has a stray parenthesis), and some equations in Theorem 1 rely on non-obvious conventions that require careful unpacking from the proof.

strengths: The central construction is elegant and technically well-executed: replacing bespoke 'nuclear-dominant' GP-on-RKHS kernels with a linear-kernel prior on the functional f plus independent GP priors on Mercer spectral coordinates of µ yields closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1), and the posterior mean provably coincides with the minimax-optimal estimator of Singh et al. (2024), positioning the method as principled uncertainty around an established estimator.

The negative analysis of BayesIMP (Appendix A.6) is a genuine contribution: Propositions 1–2 formally characterize the non-stationarity/basis-collapse of nuclear-dominant kernels and the variance-collapse of finite-dimensional approximations, with quantitative decay rates; this explains the empirical pathologies in Figs. 3–4 rather than merely observing them.

Closed-form marginal-likelihood-type objectives (Eq. 20–21) derived from the spectral decomposition, and the calibration procedure over the spectral measure with a formal consistency result (Theorem 6), go beyond simply layering a GP on top of an estimator.

The appendix is unusually thorough: measure-theoretic care (regular conditional distributions, L^2 convergence of the spectral representation via Lemma 4, Fubini/Tonelli justifications for infinite sums), data-fusion variants (Alg. 3), and incremental/average effect extensions. Honest disclosure of fixing typos in the BayesIMP baseline improves reproducibility of the comparison.

Experiments cover three distinct settings (front-door, back-door, healthcare simulator plus CBO), evaluate calibration in- and out-of-distribution, and include ablations (sample splitting, spectral measure grid, MC kernel approximation) that support the design choices.
weaknesses: The probabilistic models (10)–(11) are strong and admittedly non-structural surrogates: Y = f(ψW(W)⊗ψV(V)) + U with independent Gaussian noise, and ϕV,i(V) = µi(Z) + ξi independently across an infinite index set, will essentially never hold for real data. The paper does not analyze how misspecification of these observation models biases the posterior variance, so the coverage claims rest mainly on empirical calibration rather than theory.

The 'posterior' for γ is itself an approximation: exact moments are computed, but credible intervals come from a moment-matched GP projection minimizing KL to an intractable posterior. The paper does not quantify the error introduced by this Gaussian projection, and heavy-tailedness of the true prior (Fig. 2) suggests Gaussian intervals may be poorly shaped in principle.

Calibration requires bootstrap resampling, a grid search over the spectral measure parameter, and sample splitting — a fairly ad hoc and computationally heavy pipeline whose cost is never reported; the consistency guarantee for the calibration estimator additionally requires conditions (bootstrap consistency, Lipschitz quantiles) that are not verified in the experiments.

Empirical evaluation is limited: all causal-effect benchmarks use n = 100 synthetic samples from known simulators; the healthcare 'application' is a simulator built from a published linear model, not real observational data. Baselines are restricted to BayesIMP, a sampling GP, and one frequentist DR estimator; no comparison with modern debiased/DRML or Bayesian semiparametric approaches, and the O(n^3) scaling is never stress-tested.

Given the exact posterior-mean equivalence to Singh et al. (2024), the effective new point estimate is zero — the contribution reduces to a variance/covariance formula (S1+S2+S3) plus calibration. This is a legitimate but relatively incremental contribution whose usefulness hinges entirely on whether the approximate credible intervals are trustworthy, which is only demonstrated on small synthetic problems.

Presentation suffers from typographical and notational sloppiness that erodes confidence (e.g., 'Vdar' for V̂ar in A.6.2, unbalanced parentheses in Eqs. 15–16 and 49–50, mismatched CDF notation in Algorithm 3, 'the same for the Toy Example... Section D.2' referencing a non-existent section), and the theorem statement in the main text is dense enough that most readers must consult the appendix to verify the variance decomposition.

No discussion of a limitations section in the main text addressing when the surrogate models (10)–(11) or the spectral-measure parameterization are inappropriate, which is essential given the healthcare-motivated framing.

strengths: The core methodological idea is elegant and well-motivated: rather than constructing bespoke GP priors constrained to an RKHS (which the authors show is problematic), IMPspec expands the function class and uses spectral (Mercer) representations of the feature maps, reducing an RKHS-valued regression to a countable family of scalar GP regressions. This yields closed-form posterior moments for the causal function γ (Theorem 1) and closed-form hyperparameter objectives (MLL and WLL).

The paper convincingly demonstrates and formalizes two pathologies of the closest prior work (BayesIMP, Chau et al. 2021b): systematic underfitting caused by nonstationarity of the nuclear-dominant kernel (Propositions 1-2, Fig. 5) and posterior variance collapse under finite-dimensional approximation (Section A.6.2). This analysis is itself a valuable contribution and is backed by both theory and ablations (Table 4).

The posterior mean provably coincides with the state-of-the-art kernel estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Section A.5), so the framework is best understood as principled UQ around an established, minimax-optimal point estimator — a compelling design goal that is achieved.

The spectral calibration procedure (Algorithm 2) that tunes the free spectral measure ν to minimize credible-interval coverage error is novel, and the consistency result for the calibration estimator (Theorem 6) addresses the natural concern about combining bootstrap with plug-in estimators.

The mathematical development is careful and unusually rigorous for this area: L²-convergence of the representation (Proposition 3), justified exchange of expectations/infinite sums throughout the proof of Theorem 1, general-metric-space GP posterior (Lemma 3), and explicit data-fusion variants (Appendix A.4).

Experiments cover a toy example, a synthetic benchmark with unobserved confounding, out-of-distribution calibration evaluation, and downstream causal Bayesian optimization including a healthcare-based simulator, with ablations (sample splitting, calibration on/off, BayesIMP kernel tuning and MC approximation) that isolate the sources of improvement.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow. All experiments use n = 100–500 samples and low-dimensional settings; there is no evidence the method scales to realistic dataset sizes despite the O(n³) training/inference cost and the O(m) cost with m ≫ 10⁶ for approximating K̃_V. Stochastic minibatch variants are only mentioned, not evaluated.

Baselines are limited. The main comparison is against BayesIMP, its direct predecessor (and the authors' own reimplementation with corrected typos), plus one sampling GP and one doubly-robust estimator. There is no comparison against other modern Bayesian or conformal approaches to CATE uncertainty (e.g., other GP/DR-learner variants, conformal inference for treatment effects), which weakens the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

The model (10)–(11) is admitted to be a 'purely probabilistic surrogate' rather than a true data-generating model (notably the assumption ϕ_V,i(V) = µ_i(Z) + i.i.d. Gaussian noise with a single variance η² across all spectral coordinates). The paper does not analyze how posterior variance or credible interval validity degrades under this misspecification; the calibration procedure partially papers over this, but coverage guarantees in the misspecified regime are not established.

The calibration step is computationally expensive (grid search over spectral parameters with B bootstrap replications, each requiring full posterior recomputation) and is validated only for one parametric family ν_β = N(v̄, β²I). Sensitivity to this choice and its cost/benefit trade-off are not thoroughly explored.
No statistical convergence rates are given for the posterior itself (only mean equivalence to an estimator with known rates); the posterior variance behavior as n grows is uncharacterized.

The presentation has minor issues: several cross-references in the appendix appear inconsistent (e.g., 'see Section D.2' in C.3.2/C.3.3 when the relevant section is C.2), a code URL appears truncated/incomplete, and the density of symbols in Section 4 makes the main derivation hard to follow without the appendix.
The healthcare 'application' is a simulator built from a published linear model rather than real data, so real-world evidence for the method's claims is limited.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and technically clean: instead of forcing a GP prior to have sample paths in a prescribed RKHS (which is nontrivial and led to the pathologies of BayesIMP), the authors enlarge the function class (linear-kernel GP on f, spectral-coordinate GP priors on µ) while preserving the linear structure of the identifying formula, so the posterior mean exactly recovers the Singh et al. (2024) kernel causal estimator. This 'characterize uncertainty around an established point estimator' framing is principled.

The theoretical development is substantial and mostly rigorous: closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 4.1) with careful L2 convergence arguments for the interchange of expectation with the unbounded linear functional (Proposition C.6, Lemmas C.2/C.5), exact equivalence with scalar and vector-valued KRR (Section A.5), a novel weighted marginal-likelihood objective (22) for hyperparameter tuning, and a consistency result for the calibration-loss estimator (Theorem C.9) with an argmin-consistency argument.

The paper is unusually honest and thorough in analyzing both its own limitations (surrogate likelihood misspecification analysis in A.4, with chi-squared/TV bounds and moment perturbation bounds) and the limitations of the closest prior work (Section A.6 formalizes, with new propositions and decay rates, why BayesIMP's nuclear-dominant kernel underfits and why its finite-dimensional approximation causes out-of-support variance collapse).

Experiments are comprehensive and fair: toy example with heavy-tailed noise and limited-support variants, a standard synthetic benchmark DAG with frequentist baselines (continuous DR, ORF), causal Bayesian optimization tasks, and a 10k-sample real 401(k) case study with runtime/memory reporting. Extensive ablations (sample splitting, bootstrap count, kernel choice, spectral measure variance, BayesIMP MC approximation) strengthen the empirical claims. The favorable-but-not-strawman adaptations given to baselines (e.g., oracle offset for ORF) are commendable.

Reproducibility is good: implementation details, hyperparameters, training procedures, seeds, and evaluation metrics are documented in detail in Appendix B, and the method itself is computationally tractable (closed forms, minibatch SGD).
weaknesses: The uncertainty produced is not a genuine Bayesian posterior on the causal estimand: the likelihood (11) is explicitly a surrogate that is mis-specified by construction, and credible intervals come from a forward-KL Gaussian moment-matching. Guarantees are therefore limited to (i) recovery of the point estimator, (ii) bounds conditional on a likelihood-ratio moment condition, and (iii) consistency of the calibration-loss estimator — but there is no finite-sample or asymptotic coverage guarantee for the final intervals. The claimed 'improved uncertainty quantification' rests substantially on empirical calibration rather than theory, and calibration only tunes within a chosen spectral family.

The free spectral measure ν introduces a somewhat arbitrary knob whose role in the prior is under-theorized; the specific parametrization used in experiments (N(V̄, β²I) for continuous V) is ad hoc, and calibration reduces to a grid search whose reliability depends on bootstrap validity in finite samples.

The main theoretical object (Theorem 4.1) characterizes the posterior of the surrogate model, not the sampling distribution of the estimator; the interesting frequentist question — how the S1+S2+S3 variance relates to the estimator's true sampling variance as n grows — is not addressed.

Baselines, while reasonable, are somewhat limited: no comparison against modern CATE uncertainty approaches (e.g., Bayesian Causal Forests, DR-learner with bootstrap/conformal intervals), and the real-data case study has no ground truth, so the 401(k) experiment demonstrates feasibility rather than validity.

Some presentation issues: notation is dense (e.g., (w, w) vs (w,w') for k_W in Theorem 4.1 vs C.5), a few typos ('Vdar', mismatched parentheses in S2/S3 definitions), and the connection between the calibration objective (23) and the reported average calibration error metric requires cross-referencing Appendix B.1.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the spectral-representation trick for placing GP priors on interventional functions sidesteps known difficulties (Lukić & Beder; nuclear-dominant kernels of Flaxman et al. and BayesIMP) and the analysis of why BayesIMP underfits (Propositions A.10/A.11, variance collapse in A.6.2) is itself a useful contribution.

The posterior mean provably recovers the established kernel estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Section A.5), which grounds the uncertainty quantification in a well-studied point estimator rather than an ad hoc surrogate.

Careful technical treatment: the L2-justification for exchanging expectation with the unbounded linear functional (Prop. C.6), the likelihood-ratio-based bounds on posterior distortion from the surrogate likelihood (A.4), and the consistency result for the calibration estimator (Thm. C.9) are thorough and mostly correct-looking.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: toy example, synthetic DAG benchmark, CBO tasks on a healthcare simulator, 401(k) real-data case study, plus extensive ablations (sample splitting, bootstrap replications, kernel choice, heavy-tailed noise, limited support, baseline fixes).
Honest limitations discussion and impact statement; implementation details are unusually complete, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method rests on an admittedly misspecified surrogate likelihood (11). The bounds in A.4 are conditional on a moment-control assumption on the likelihood ratio (E[R^2]/E[R]^2 ≤ 1+ε) that is never verified or estimated in practice, so the mis-specification analysis provides little practical assurance about the reported posterior variances.

Calibration tunes only a single scalar parameter (the spectral-measure scale β). This can rescale posterior variance but cannot correct structural misfit; consequently the 'calibrated' intervals lack any frequentist coverage guarantee, and consistency of grid-search calibration (Thm. C.9) requires assumptions (Lipschitzness of F_α, consistency of bootstrap plus plug-in) that are not established for the actual estimator pipeline.

The 'spectral measure ν' is essentially an extra hyperparameter with weak conceptual grounding; the calibration objective (23) evaluated on a bootstrap plug-in makes coverage claims somewhat circular, and the calibration procedure is computationally heavy (bootstrap × grid search, each requiring O(n^3) GP fits).

Empirical gains over the main GP baseline (BayesIMP) are partly attributable to pathologies specific to BayesIMP's kernel construction; the improvements over the sampling GP and continuous DR baselines in Table 2 are moderate, and in the limited-support setting the sampling GP beats IMPspec on RMSE.

Results are reported without statistical significance testing of method differences; several margins (e.g., IMPspec vs. BayesIMP RMSE in Table 2: 0.36 ± 0.16 vs. 0.38 ± 0.13) are within noise, so the strongest claims ('improves uncertainty quantification') are only clearly supported for calibration error.
Heavy dependence on prior work (Singh et al., 2024; Chau et al., 2021b) for the underlying estimation framework and problem setup, which somewhat narrows the standalone novelty.

strengths: Well-motivated and important problem: uncertainty quantification for function-valued causal targets (CATE, dose-response, ATT) is a genuine gap; existing frequentist approaches require extra structure and GP priors on prescribed RKHSs are known to be nontrivial.

Technically sound and creative core idea: the spectral (Mercer) representation of the feature map reduces the infinite-dimensional RKHS-valued function μ(z) to scalar conditional expectations on which standard GP priors can be placed, avoiding the pathologies of the nuclear-dominant kernels in BayesIMP (underfitting from nonstationarity; variance collapse from finite-dimensional approximation). The relaxed linear-kernel prior on f is a clean solution to the GP-samples-not-in-RKHS problem.

The design choice that the posterior mean provably coincides with the established kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Theorem 4.1, Appendix A.5) is valuable: the method characterizes uncertainty around an estimator with known minimax rates rather than introducing a new point estimator, making the contribution easy to adopt and interpret.

Complete practical pipeline: closed-form posterior moments (mean, variance, covariance for incremental effects, and GP projections for ATEs), marginal-likelihood hyperparameter tuning including a novel tractable weighted spectral likelihood (22), and a bootstrap calibration procedure with a consistency result (Theorem C.9) and a sample-splitting ablation.

Thorough and honest treatment of the closest prior work: the analysis of BayesIMP limitations (Propositions A.10–A.11 with decay rates, Figure 7, ablations in Table 5 including fixing two typos in the original implementation, which is disclosed) substantiates the claimed pathologies rather than merely asserting them.

Broad evaluation: toy front-door data-fusion task, synthetic benchmark DAG against frequentist baselines (Kennedy et al. 2017, ORF) with in- and out-of-support calibration analysis, causal Bayesian optimization tasks including a healthcare simulator built from real estimates, and a large-scale 401(k) case study with runtime/memory feasibility. Multiple ablations (bootstrap replications, kernel choice, heavy-tailed noise, limited support) support robustness.
The limitations section is candid about surrogate Gaussian likelihoods, moment-matched GP approximation, and calibration being confined to a chosen spectral family.
weaknesses: The posterior is constructed under surrogate likelihoods; the additive Gaussian model (11) on Mercer coordinates is a strong modeling assumption (exact only for linear kernels with Gaussian noise). The mis-specification analysis in A.4 is generic — it assumes the likelihood-ratio moment condition E[R^2]/E[R]^2 ≤ 1+ε without verifying or estimating it for the actual model, so the resulting bounds are largely conceptual rather than a quantitative guarantee.

Frequentist coverage of the credible intervals has no guarantee; calibration tunes only a scalar scale of the spectral measure within a restricted family (N(V̄, β²I)), so coverage improvements are necessarily limited, and the consistency result for the calibration loss is conditional on assumptions (Lipschitzness of F_α, plug-in consistency) that are not verified in the experiments.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the GP–KRR posterior-mean equivalence is known (Kanagawa et al. 2018), and the point estimator is exactly Singh et al. (2024); the genuinely new pieces are the spectral μ prior, the closed-form covariance terms, the WLL objective, and the calibration loop — a useful but not groundbreaking extension.

Empirical gains over the strongest competitors are moderate; on the synthetic benchmark BayesIMP is close in RMSE (0.38 vs 0.36), and under limited treatment support Sampling-GP achieves lower RMSE. Results are at small n (100–500) over 50 trials; the real-data study has no ground truth, so it only supports plausibility, not validity.

Computational cost is substantial: O(n³) objectives, bootstrap-based calibration requiring repeated refits (54.5s of the ~68s total on 401(k)), limiting scalability; sparse approximations are deferred to future work.

Presentation issues in the appendix: inconsistent numbering (assumptions/remarks referred to as 'Theorem A.1', 'Theorem A.9'), typos (e.g., 'Vdar', malformed variance expression in the BayesIMP analysis on p.23), and heavy reliance on the appendix for core derivations, which slightly impedes readability of the main results.

The KL-minimization interpretation of the moment-matched GP (forward KL) is stated but not deeply exploited; the theoretical role of the Gaussian projection in the total error decomposition is left with an unbounded TV(P̂, P̃) term.
